title: The First World War: causes, practices and effects
summary: The long- and short-term causes of the 1914 war, the July Crisis debate, how the war was fought as total war, and the peace settlements that followed.

keyterms.definition: The Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain) dividing Europe before 1914.
Anglo-German competition in battleship building, intensified after Britain launched HMS Dreadnought in 1906.
Diplomatic crisis between the Sarajevo assassination (28 June 1914) and the outbreak of general war in early August.
Germany's promise in early July 1914 to back Austria-Hungary unconditionally in action against Serbia.
German plan to defeat France quickly through Belgium before turning on Russia; it brought Britain into the war.
Fritz Fischer's 1961 argument that Germany's leaders sought expansion and bore main responsibility for the war.
War in which states mobilise their whole society and economy, and civilians become targets, e.g. through blockade and conscription.
Strategy of wearing down the enemy through continuous losses, typical of Western Front battles such as Verdun.
Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles, assigning Germany and its allies responsibility for loss and damage, the basis for reparations.
Principle, championed by Woodrow Wilson, that nations should govern themselves; applied unevenly in 1919.

lessons.title: Causes of the First World War

questions.prompt: Put these events of the July Crisis in order.
questions.explanation: 28 June, 5–6 July, 23 July, 28 July, 4 August 1914.

questions.prompt: Why did Britain declare war on 4 August 1914?
options: Germany invaded neutral Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed in 1839
questions.explanation: The Schlieffen Plan's route through Belgium turned a continental war into a world war.

questions.text: Britain launched HMS ___ in 1906, intensifying the naval race.
questions.explanation: Its design made earlier battleships obsolete, letting Germany compete on more equal terms.

questions.prompt: Match each pre-war crisis to its significance.

pairs.right: Austria annexed Bosnia, humiliating Russia and Serbia
German gunboat sent; Britain backed France

questions.explanation: Each crisis hardened the alliances and raised tensions in the Balkans.

questions.statement: Fritz Fischer argued that Germany deliberately pursued aggressive war aims in 1914.
questions.explanation: His 'Griff nach der Weltmacht' (1961) used German documents such as the September Programme; it caused a major controversy in West Germany.

questions.prompt: Which historian argued in 'The Sleepwalkers' (2012) that responsibility was shared among the powers?
questions.explanation: Clark stressed miscalculation and the role of Serbia, Russia and France alongside Germany and Austria-Hungary.

questions.text: Germany's war plan to defeat France through Belgium was the ___ Plan.
questions.explanation: It required Germany to attack France as soon as Russia mobilised, limiting diplomacy.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why Russian general mobilisation (30 July) was so significant?
options: German plans treated it as making war inevitable, triggering their attack on France
It meant Russia had invaded Austria
It forced Italy to join Germany
questions.explanation: Military timetables turned mobilisation into a trigger; Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August.

questions.statement: Italy fought alongside Germany in 1914 as a member of the Triple Alliance.
questions.explanation: Italy stayed neutral, arguing the alliance was defensive, and joined the Entente in 1915 after the Treaty of London.

questions.prompt: Which is a long-term rather than a short-term cause of the war?
options: German declaration of war on Russia
questions.explanation: Strong essays distinguish underlying causes from triggers and assess how they interacted.

lessons.title: Fighting the war and its effects

questions.prompt: Why did the Western Front become a stalemate of trenches by late 1914?
options: Defensive firepower (machine guns, artillery) outmatched attacking forces after the Marne
Both sides ran out of soldiers
questions.explanation: After the Battle of the Marne (September 1914) and the 'race to the sea', trenches stretched from the Channel to Switzerland.

questions.text: German commander Falkenhayn aimed to 'bleed France white' at ___ in 1916.
questions.explanation: Verdun was a battle of attrition lasting most of 1916, with huge losses on both sides.

questions.statement: The British army suffered about 57,000 casualties on the first day of the Somme, 1 July 1916.
questions.explanation: Around 19,000 were killed, the heaviest single-day loss in British military history.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
questions.explanation: September 1914, April 1915, July 1916, April 1917, 11 November 1918.

questions.prompt: What brought the USA into the war in April 1917?
options: Germany's resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram
questions.explanation: Germany gambled it could starve Britain before US troops arrived in large numbers.

questions.prompt: Match each treaty to the defeated state.
questions.explanation: Sèvres was rejected by Turkish nationalists and replaced by the Treaty of Lausanne (1923).

questions.text: Article ___ of the Treaty of Versailles is known as the war guilt clause.
questions.explanation: Germans saw it as a humiliating 'Diktat', fuelling resentment exploited by nationalists.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of total war on the home front?
options: Conscription, rationing and women working in munitions factories
Professional armies fighting far from civilians
A war limited to one battle
questions.explanation: States took control of industry, labour and propaganda; the British naval blockade caused severe hunger in Germany.

questions.statement: Four empires collapsed as a result of the First World War: German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman.
questions.explanation: New states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia emerged in central and eastern Europe.

questions.prompt: Why did Germany seek an armistice in autumn 1918?
options: Its spring offensive had failed, Allied counter-attacks were advancing and its allies were collapsing
questions.explanation: The Hundred Days offensive from August 1918, blockade and unrest at home forced Germany to ask for terms.
